lesson_title: Strong Is Not Concentrated: Acids, Bases and pH
hook_text: Your kitchen vinegar is CONCENTRATED. Pool-test acid is STRONG. No — those are not the same thing.
clip_script: Two bottles. One is kitchen vinegar — packed with acid, and mostly harmless on your slap chips. The other holds a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid — barely any acid at all, yet every single molecule of it is armed. Here's the distinction that upgrades your chemistry marks: strong is not concentrated. Concentration is how much acid is in the bottle. Strength is how WILLING each molecule is to hand over its proton — because that is all an acid is, a proton giver, and a base is a proton taker. Strong acids like hydrochloric give completely: every molecule donates, pH drops hard. Weak acids like the ethanoic acid in vinegar are reluctant: only a few percent let go, the rest sit intact. Same concentration, totally different pH — and chemists score the willingness with one number, K a. Big K a, eager. Tiny K a, stubborn. Then the ladder: pH. Every step is a factor of TEN. A river dropping from pH 6 to 4 didn't get 'a bit' more acidic — it got a hundred times more acidic, and the fish know it. Amount in the bottle, willingness to give, and a ladder of tens — hold those three apart and the whole topic opens up.
visual_style: Two bottles side by side with molecule close-ups — one crowd of intact reluctant molecules, one sparse squad all split into glowing ions; a pH ladder where each rung multiplies a crowd counter by ten.
mood: Myth-busting and crisp — one everyday confusion dismantled.
pacing: Two-bottle cold open, quick giver-taker beat, split-screen strength reveal, ladder-of-tens finale.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and take the factor-of-two trap out of your pH calculations for good.
